title: The reader: giving every letter a meaning
blurb: The reader is a borrowed part. It reads the question once and gives every letter a meaning in context.

scenes.heading: Where we are: the reader comes first

caption.text: The question enters the reader first. The reader is a borrowed model called Gemma, and it reads the whole question one time.
Picture only: a translator who already knows English well. We borrowed him, and we cannot change him.

scenes.heading: The reader reads once, then copies meaning

caption.text: Gemma reads the whole question one time.
Each token gets a row of 768 numbers that holds its meaning in context.
Each letter takes the row of the token it sits in.

scenes.heading: Four parts added into one letter row

caption.text: First: which letter it is. A learned row of numbers.
Second: where it sits in the question. A learned table: 2,000 rows in the planned finished design (B3), 280 in the growth test (G1).
Third: how far its letter sits from the end of its word. The count is hand-written; the row it picks is learned.
Fourth: Gemma's meaning, through the converter plug, is added on top. Then the letter window (next scene) reads the sum.

scenes.heading: The letter window: each letter sees 4 each side

caption.text: Two small learned layers read the summed row. They are ours, not borrowed.
Each layer looks 2 letters left and 2 right, so together a letter sees 4 letters each side.
The window adds about 0.7 million numbers at width 256, about 2.6 million at 512.
